title: Awakenings and Enlightenment
subtitle: From the exhaustion of Westphalia to the first religious free market. Pietism's answer to cold orthodoxy, the Enlightenment's rival account, Edwards and Whitefield and Wesley, and the forging of the tools America would later mistake for the move of God.

sections.title: The Peace of Exhaustion
sections.body:
In 1648 Europe stopped fighting about God. Not because anyone had won. The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years War the way exhaustion ends most things, with an arrangement rather than a verdict: each ruler would set the religion of his own territory, Lutheran and Reformed and Catholic would learn to exist on the same map, and the continent, bled nearly white, agreed to coexist because it could no longer afford to kill. Germany had lost, by the common reckoning, something like a third of its people. Whole regions had been marched over, burned over, and taxed into famine by armies that all claimed heaven. When the diplomats finally signed, nobody pretended the truth had been settled. They had simply run out of blood to spend on it.

What followed inside the Protestant churches is usually told with a sneer, and the sneer is not entirely fair. The generations after the Reformation built systems. Lutheran and Reformed theologians organized the recovered gospel into massive, careful bodies of doctrine, defining every term, answering every objection, guarding every border. Say it honestly: this was serious work by serious men, and much of what later Christians casually believe was kept safe in those systems the way grain is kept safe in a stone barn. A church that had just watched Europe tear itself apart over doctrine had reasons to want its doctrine exact.

But something cooled while the walls went up. Where every subject of a territory was baptized into its church by law, membership stopped meaning conversion and started meaning residence. The sermon drifted toward the lecture, the faith toward correct assent, the pastor toward the professor. A man could be catechized, confirmed, married, and buried in perfect orthodoxy without anyone ever asking whether he knew the God he could define. The critics inside the church would soon have a name for this, dead orthodoxy, and like most polemical names it was unfair to the best and accurate about the rest.

I am careful with this history because it is not safely in the past. I have preached sermons that were correct in every clause and cost me nothing, and I have sat with church members who could pass a doctrine exam and could not pray. A church can be exactly right and fast asleep. Seventeenth-century Germany did not invent that condition. It only built an unusually well-documented version of it.

The wars ended in 1648. The weariness did not. It settled into the pews and stayed for a generation, and the modern era opened with Europe holding a faith it was no longer sure it felt, defended by systems it no longer loved. Two very different answers were coming, one from inside the church and one from outside it, and between them they would shape everything this library still has to tell.

sections.title: The Answer of the Heart
sections.body:
The answer from inside came from a Frankfurt pastor named Philipp Jakob Spener, and it came in the form of a preface. In 1675 Spener was asked to introduce a new edition of a beloved devotional writer, and what he wrote outgrew the assignment and was published on its own as Pia Desideria, pious desires, a small book with a modest tone and a program that would not stay small. Spener did not attack the church's doctrine. He assumed it. His charge was that the doctrine had stopped reaching the heart, and his proposals were almost embarrassingly practical: get the whole Bible into the hands of ordinary people, not just the preaching texts; gather believers in small circles in homes to read Scripture together and speak of their souls; take seriously the old Reformation claim that every believer is a priest, so that the laity carry the faith rather than merely attend it; train pastors in devotion and not only disputation; conduct controversy with charity; preach for the building of people rather than the display of learning.

None of this sounds radical until you notice what it assumes, which is that a person baptized into a state church may still need to be converted, and that the real church might be a warm circle inside the cold institution. Spener's little gatherings, the collegia pietatis, were the ancestors of every small group meeting in a living room tonight, and the movement they seeded came to be called Pietism, a name first used, like Methodist and Christian before it, as an insult.

Pietism built. August Hermann Francke turned the university town of Halle into a working demonstration of what warmed faith does with its hands: an orphanage founded in 1695, schools for the poor, a publishing operation, a dispensary, and in 1706 the sending of the first Protestant missionaries to India, two Halle men to the Danish post at Tranquebar. And a generation later a young nobleman raised in that Halle world, Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf, let a band of persecuted Moravian refugees settle on his estate. The village they built, Herrnhut, was quarrelsome and fragile until the summer of 1727, when a communion service turned into something the community could only call a visitation of the Spirit. Out of that renewal came a prayer watch the Moravians kept going around the clock for generations, and out of the prayer came missionaries: to the enslaved Africans of the Caribbean in 1732, to Greenland the year after, outward from a village of a few hundred souls to places the great state churches had never bothered to go. The Moravians will matter to this story again, because a discouraged Anglican priest is going to meet them on a ship in an Atlantic storm.

Weigh Pietism fairly, both hands. It recovered something the systems had buried: the expectation that God actually converts people, that faith is a life and not only a position, that laypeople are the church rather than its audience. Nearly everything warm in modern Protestant devotion descends from it. But every correction carries the seed of its own excess, and the seed in this one is visible from here. A faith relocated to the heart can come loose from the head that anchored it; the warm circle can learn to treat feeling as its own evidence. Spener never made that trade, and it is no accident that the man who later taught Protestant theology to ground itself in religious feeling itself, Friedrich Schleiermacher, was schooled by the Moravians. The grandchildren kept the warmth and, some of them, sold the house.

Hold the balance and do not sneer in either direction. Cold orthodoxy and untethered warmth are both real failures, and the church has spent three centuries lurching between them. Pietism, at its source, refused the choice. It wanted the creed and the converted heart, the stone barn and the living grain. That refusal is the part worth keeping.

sections.title: The Rival Account of Everything
sections.body:
The answer from outside the church was larger, and the church has spent three hundred years pretending it did not partly deserve it.

Begin with what the men of the Enlightenment had actually watched. Their grandfathers' Europe had burned dissenters, coerced consciences with the sword, and fought a thirty-year war in which every army marched under God's name. Confessional states had made doubt a civil crime and turned the map of Europe into a patchwork of compulsory certainties. Meanwhile a different kind of knowledge was succeeding spectacularly. In 1687 Isaac Newton, himself a God-haunted man and no skeptic, published the Principia and showed that the same mathematics governed a falling apple and an orbiting moon. The universe, it turned out, ran on law, and the law could be found by any patient mind regardless of its catechism. Set the two pictures side by side, as the eighteenth century did. Religion, enforced by magistrates, had produced a century of blood. Reason, enforced by nothing, was producing knowledge that worked in every country at once. If you had lived then, you might have drawn the same conclusion they drew.

So state their case at full strength, because it deserves it. The Enlightenment proposed that human beings should dare to think for themselves rather than under license, that authority must give reasons, that cruelty in God's name is still cruelty, and that a truth which requires the rack to sustain it has already confessed something about itself. John Locke argued in 1695 that Christianity, rightly read, was reasonable. The deists went further: God as the great designer who built the machine, wound it, and stepped back, leaving a religion of nature and morality that any honest mind could reach without priest or miracle. Books like John Toland's Christianity Not Mysterious in 1696 and Matthew Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation in 1730 pressed the program, and by 1784 Immanuel Kant could sum up the whole era with a motto borrowed from the Roman poet Horace, sapere aude, dare to know, and could later title a book with the era's ambition for faith itself: religion within the limits of reason alone. Gotthold Lessing, the German critic, named the deepest problem with disarming honesty: between the accidental truths of history, a man crucified under Pontius Pilate, and the necessary truths of reason stood a ditch he confessed he could not leap. Revelation claims that everything hangs on particular events; reason, as the age defined it, could only certify what holds everywhere and always.

The confidence cracked before the century ended. On the morning of All Saints Day, 1755, while the churches of Lisbon were full for the feast, an earthquake leveled the city and killed tens of thousands, and Voltaire wrote his furious poem asking what optimism about the great design was worth now. The question cut both ways, though the age rarely noticed: it was a hard question for providence, and a harder one for a religion of nature whose god had no cross, no presence in suffering, and nothing to say at a mass grave except that the machine ran on.

Here is what must be said from inside the church, and said without flinching. The Enlightenment saw real corruption and named it truly. Coerced faith, clerical privilege, holy cruelty, the marriage of altar and throne: those were not slanders, they were observations, and the men who made them were often more honest about the church than the church was about itself. When reason applied for the job of referee above the warring confessions, it was applying for a position the churches had visibly failed to fill. We handed our critics their evidence. That is the confession.

And here is what the new account could not see. It diagnosed the church's cruelty and misread the human heart, treating evil as ignorance, curable by education, and progress as the natural drift of enlightened man. The next two centuries would run the experiment at scale, and the results are not in reason's favor. Scripture had made the darker and, it turns out, the more accurate claim all along, that wisdom begins in the fear of the LORD and that a mind can be brilliant and bent at the same time. The Enlightenment got the symptom right and the anthropology wrong. But a church that only says that sentence, and never says the one before it, has learned nothing from the century that produced its sharpest critics. Both sentences are true. The order matters: confession first.

sections.title: The Surprising Work at Northampton
sections.body:
While Europe argued, something happened in a Massachusetts river town, and the man it happened around spent the rest of his life trying to be honest about it.

Jonathan Edwards was the pastor of Northampton, heir to his grandfather's long ministry there and, by wide agreement since, the most formidable theological mind America has produced. In December of 1734, in the middle of a sermon series on justification by faith alone, his town began to change. Conversions came in ones and twos and then in waves, and by spring the awakening had touched, by Edwards's own account, every part of the town, the old and the young, the respectable and the rough. His report of it, A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God, was published in London in 1737 with the endorsement of two leading English ministers, and it did something no colonial pamphlet had done before: it taught the whole Atlantic world to expect that God might suddenly move on an ordinary town, and it gave that expectation a shape, almost a script. Revival now had a literature. The importance of that fact will take a century to fully unfold.

The Northampton awakening ended in grief, and Edwards did not hide it. In 1735 his own uncle, a prominent man of the town who had fallen into a deep and settled despair, took his own life, and the fervor broke like a fever. Edwards recorded it in the Narrative itself. He would not sell a version of the story with the wound cut out, and that refusal is the first thing to learn from him.

The second is larger. When awakening returned to New England at the turn of the 1740s, larger and wilder than before, Edwards became its defender, and then he became something rarer: its examiner. In 1741, at Yale, he preached The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God, arguing that a true work of God is not disproved by noise, excess, and error around its edges, any more than a real harvest is disproved by chaff. But the same argument cut the other way, and in 1746, in Religious Affections, he turned the blade fully around. True religion, he argued, does consist in holy affections; the Enlightenment's cool assent is not conversion. And yet almost nothing that revival produces on its surface proves anything at all. Tears prove nothing. Trembling proves nothing. Visions, transports, fluent testimonies, bodily effects, the loudest assurance in the room: nothing. The signs that matter are of another kind entirely, a new sense of God's beauty, humility that deepens over time, and above all what he placed last and highest, holy practice, a life that keeps obeying when the feeling has gone. He was doing in a book what the apostle John had commanded in a sentence: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1).

Hold the two Edwardses together, because American Christianity would later insist on splitting them. The man who defended revival against its cultured despisers and the man who tested revival down to its foundations were the same man, doing the same work. He believed God had genuinely moved, and precisely because he believed it, he refused to let the heat certify itself. The fire and the assay, together.

Edwards was no performer. He preached closely from his manuscript in a level voice, a fact worth remembering when you hear about the most famous sermon in American history, Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, preached at Enfield in July 1741, remembered for its terror, delivered without theatrics while the congregation cried out. Whatever happened in that meetinghouse, it was not stagecraft.

And then the ending, which every pastor should be made to sit with. In 1750 the town that had been famous on two continents for the surprising work of God dismissed its pastor. The break came over communion: Edwards had concluded he could no longer admit to the table those who made no credible profession of faith, reversing his own grandfather's practice, and Northampton, awakened Northampton, voted him out. He went to the frontier at Stockbridge as a missionary to the Mohican and Mohawk people, wrote the works that made him immortal, accepted the presidency of Princeton, and died there in 1758 after a smallpox inoculation. The town of the revival fired the man who told it what revival required. Awakening, it turns out, does not automatically become formation. That sentence is one of the two or three this whole era exists to teach.

sections.title: The First Celebrity Preacher
sections.body:
George Whitefield grew up in a Gloucester tavern, worked his way through Oxford as a servant to wealthier students, and discovered in his twenties that he possessed the most extraordinary voice of his age. What he did with it changed the shape of Protestant Christianity more than any doctrine argued in this period, and the change was not doctrinal at all.

In February 1739, shut out of Bristol pulpits that found him too hot, the young ordained Anglican walked out to Kingswood and preached in the open air to coal miners, men no parish had ever gone looking for. He wrote in his journal of watching their tears cut streaks through the coal dust on their faces. Within weeks the crowds had grown from hundreds to thousands, and Whitefield had learned the lesson of his life: the church was no longer the necessary container of preaching. The field, the market cross, the town common, anywhere a crowd could stand was now a sanctuary, and a crowd could be gathered by the same means that gathered one for anything else.

He used those means with a genius the modern reader will recognize instantly. Advance men rode ahead to book venues and stir interest, his friend William Seward feeding the newspapers reports of the crowds before and after they gathered. His journals were published serially, installments of an unfolding story with himself at the center. Controversy was not avoided but courted, since attacks in print filled fields better than praise. He crossed the Atlantic thirteen times, itinerating through America in tours that stitched thirteen separate colonies into a single audience; historians have called him, with only slight exaggeration, the first person famous in the same way across the whole English-speaking world. When he preached his farewell on Boston Common in 1740, contemporaries reckoned the crowd larger than the population of Boston itself.

His unlikeliest friend is the best witness. Benjamin Franklin, printer, skeptic, no man's fool, published Whitefield's journals in Philadelphia, made money doing it, and studied the phenomenon with a naturalist's eye. In his Autobiography, Franklin describes pacing out the distance at which the preacher's voice stayed distinct and computing that more than thirty thousand people could hear him in the open air, a fact he noted because he had disbelieved the newspaper crowds until he did the arithmetic. He also records, with a smile you can still hear, resolving before an orphanage sermon to give nothing, then softening as Whitefield preached until he emptied his pocket into the plate, coppers, silver, and gold together. The two men remained affectionate friends for thirty years. Franklin wrote that Whitefield used to pray for his conversion, but never had the satisfaction of believing his prayers were heard. The greatest evangelist of the century loved a skeptic honestly for thirty years and could not talk him in. The friendship was still worth having, and Whitefield seems never to have doubted it. There is a lesson in that for a platform like this one, and I do not intend to hurry past it.

The historian Harry Stout has pressed a harder reading, and it deserves its hearing. Whitefield had been stagestruck as a schoolboy, trained in the actor's arts he later renounced, and Stout's argument, in The Divine Dramatist, is that he never really renounced them: that he carried the theater's techniques of voice, gesture, tears, and dramatic persona into the pulpit, invented the religious celebrity, and marketed the new birth in the same commercial idiom the eighteenth century was learning to market everything else. You can quarrel with the emphasis. Whitefield's sincerity is not really in doubt, his doctrine was Calvinist and cross-centered, and thousands of the conversions held for a lifetime. But the technique is not in doubt either. Event, crowd, publicity, celebrity, serial content, the itinerant star unaccountable to any congregation: all of it was assembled here, by a sincere man, for the glory of God. The genie did not look like a genie. It looked like revival.

One more fact, and it must not be softened, because it points straight at the next essay. Whitefield's beloved Bethesda orphanage in Georgia was, he judged, impossible to sustain without enslaved labor, and so the most famous Christian in the English-speaking world campaigned publicly for the legalization of slavery in the one colony that had banned it. Georgia legalized it, and Bethesda ran on the labor of enslaved people Whitefield bought. He had preached to the enslaved, defended their souls' full capacity against planters who doubted it, and then purchased human beings to fund the work of God. The means served the end; the end justified the means. Remember the shape of that reasoning. America is about to build a century on it.

sections.title: A Warmed Heart and a Working System
sections.body:
John Wesley's story begins with a failure that reads like a comedy until you feel it. An Oxford don of ferocious discipline, founder with his brother Charles of the Holy Club that mocking students called Methodist, he sailed to Georgia in 1735 to convert the Indians and returned in 1737 having converted no one, fleeing a church discipline case that grew out of a courtship he had handled badly. On the voyage over, in an Atlantic storm that snapped the mast and had English passengers screaming, he had watched a company of Moravian families calmly singing psalms, children included, and he could not forget it. He had crossed an ocean to bring the gospel and met people who plainly had something he did not.

Back in London, the Moravian Peter Böhler pressed him with the old Pietist question, whether he had saving faith or only the doctrine of it. The answer came on 24 May 1738, at a society meeting in Aldersgate Street, where someone was reading Luther's preface to Romans. Wesley recorded it in his Journal with a clock-time precision that has kept the moment alive for three centuries: "about a quarter before nine," while the reader described the change God works in the heart through faith, "I felt my heart strangely warmed." He felt, he wrote, that he did now trust Christ alone for salvation. What converted him was not a crowd or a stage. It was a small room, an old book, a handful of believers. The instrument of Aldersgate was the thing Spener had proposed in 1675.

Within a year Whitefield had summoned him to Bristol and to a practice that scandalized his churchmanship. Wesley's Journal entry for 2 April 1739 records that he "submitted to be more vile" and preached in the open air for the first time, to the same Kingswood colliers. He took to field preaching for the rest of his life, riding, by any reckoning, a staggering number of miles across Britain for half a century, and when clergy objected that he was invading their parishes he answered, in substance, that he looked upon the whole world as his parish.

Aldersgate is not what makes Wesley the hinge of this era. The system is. Whitefield gathered crowds and moved on. Wesley gathered crowds and then organized them. Every person awakened under Methodist preaching was pressed into a society, and every society was divided into classes of about a dozen, meeting weekly under a leader, every member answering in turn for the week, sins, temptations, graces, by name, face to face. The class meeting began prosaically, in Bristol in 1742, as a scheme for retiring a building debt a penny a week, and Wesley recognized within weeks that he had stumbled onto the thing itself: a machinery of watching over one another in love. Beyond the classes were bands for those who wanted closer accountability. Membership was by ticket, renewed quarterly, and the tickets of the unrepentant were quietly not renewed. Wesley pruned his societies without embarrassment, reporting membership losses in his journals as soberly as gains, because the number that mattered to him was not attendance. Lay preachers rode circuits and were themselves examined annually at a conference, held first in 1744. And the whole apparatus bent outward: the societies visited prisons, fed the poor, ran schools and dispensaries; days before his death in 1791, Wesley's last letter urged the young William Wilberforce onward in the parliamentary war against the slave trade.

The historian David Bebbington, in Evangelicalism in Modern Britain, gave the movement born in these decades its now-standard definition, four marks: conversion, the Bible, the cross, and activism, the insistence that the gospel goes to work. By that definition, evangelicalism as such begins here, in the 1730s, and Wesley and Whitefield are its founding pair. But the pair embodied two different futures. They quarreled bitterly over predestination in 1741, healed the friendship, and Wesley preached at Whitefield's memorial service in 1770 at the dead man's own request. The deeper divergence was never doctrinal. Whitefield perfected the awakening as event. Wesley bound the awakening to a discipline, the crowd dissolved each week into small rooms where people were known by name and asked how it actually stood with their souls. Awakening with formation. The event with the hearth.

Both men believed God had moved, and I believe it too. The question the next century would answer, mostly in the dark, was which of them America would imitate. It is not a spoiler to say that the crowds were easier to copy than the classes.

sections.title: Old Lights and New
sections.body:
The awakening split New England, and the split deserves to be told fairly, because both sides were guarding something real and both sides lost something they did not intend to lose.

Begin with the man who handed the critics their case. James Davenport was a young minister swept up in the revival who became its caricature: itinerating through towns to declare, by name, which settled pastors he judged unconverted, urging congregations to leave their churches, working crowds into frenzies past anything Edwards defended. In March 1743 at New London he led his followers in burning a pile of religious books by respected authors, and the next day called for a bonfire of fine clothes, stripping off his own breeches to add them, at which point even his own followers balked. The year after, chastened and ill, he published a public confession retracting nearly all of it. He was not the awakening. But he was visible, and he was exactly what its opponents needed.

Charles Chauncy of Boston's First Church became the voice of those opponents, the Old Lights, and his case, laid out in Seasonable Thoughts on the State of Religion in New England in 1743, is stronger than revivalist history likes to admit. State it the way he would: God is a God of order, not confusion. An affection stirred by a skilled voice in a mass of strangers is evidence of nothing but the skill and the mass; the passions are the lowest part of a man and the easiest to play. Itinerant strangers were slandering faithful pastors, dividing congregations that had taken a century to build, and teaching people to treat an experience they could date as more certain than a life they could examine. Every one of those sentences names a real danger. Edwards himself conceded most of them in the act of answering him.

The New Light answer, Edwards's answer, was the one already described: judge the work by its lasting fruit, not its noise; a true work of God has never once come to human beings without human mess around it; and a church that waits for a revival with no excesses is waiting for a revival with no people. Where Chauncy saw the passions being played, Edwards saw, beneath the froth he freely admitted, actual lives turning to God and staying turned.

Both were partly right. That is not a diplomatic dodge; it is the verdict of the evidence. The excesses were real, and they discredited revival among the educated for a generation. The conversions were real too, and they filled churches with people for whom Christianity had become a fact of experience and not only of inheritance. What neither side intended was what the quarrel taught America: that order and fire are opposites, and a Christian must choose. Edwards had spent his best books refusing exactly that choice. The country took the choice and left the books.

The later paths of the two parties are instructive, and the instruction cuts both ways, so let it cut. Chauncy's stream, the party of order and reason, drifted over two generations toward a religion of morality and benevolence; Chauncy himself argued in print at the end of his life for universal salvation, and the churches of his party in eastern Massachusetts became, in time, Unitarian. The party that feared enthusiasm cooled past Christianity. And the revival stream fractured into Separate congregations that abandoned the established churches, many of which became Baptist, carried south by men like Shubal Stearns, whose Sandy Creek church in North Carolina, planted in 1755, seeded congregations across the backcountry. I note without embarrassment that this is my own family line: the Baptist multiplication in the South came out of this fire. The party that feared coldness would eventually, in some of its heirs, learn to manufacture heat. Neither drift was necessary. Both happened.

Somewhere under the quarrel lies the question this whole library keeps returning to, and it is worth stating plainly here because the next essay depends on it. When something powerful happens in a crowd, what exactly happened? The eighteenth century forced that question into the open and produced, in Edwards, the most careful answer the church has ever given. The nineteenth would largely stop asking.

sections.title: The First Free Market of Faith
sections.body:
The last act of this era happened in law, and my own people helped write it from the inside of jails.

In the Virginia of the 1760s and 1770s, the established Church of England still held legal privilege, and Baptist preachers who would not seek its license were beaten by mobs and locked up by magistrates, dozens of them across those years. They preached anyway. James Ireland, jailed at Culpeper in the winter of 1769, went on preaching through the bars of his cell window to the crowd outside, and his memoir records the attempts to stop him, including an effort to smoke him out of the window with burning pepper. The spectacle of men imprisoned for sermons did something to Virginia's conscience, and it did something particular to a young James Madison, who knew of dissenting preachers jailed near his own county and never forgot it. When the Revolution came, the Baptists of Virginia, with Presbyterians beside them, pressed the new commonwealth to end religious establishment altogether, and they found their allies in men who did not share their theology at all. Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance of 1785 argued that religion can be directed only by reason and conviction, not by force; Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom, enacted in 1786, wrote it into law; Jefferson counted it among the three achievements on his gravestone. In 1791 the First Amendment carried the principle into the federal constitution. Massachusetts, characteristically, kept its establishment until 1833. But the direction was set, and it was new in the history of the world: a nation with no church at all, where every congregation stood on its own persuasion and its own collection plate.

Be fair to what this was. Disestablishment was not secularism's victory over faith; it was, in large part, faith's victory over coerced faith, argued by Baptists out of Anabaptist blood and out of the New Testament's plain picture of a church you cannot be born into but must be born again into. Men like Isaac Backus in Massachusetts and the jailed preachers of Virginia believed establishment corrupted the church more than it protected her, and seventeen centuries of evidence stood behind them. The awakening had made the case existentially: if the true church is the company of the converted, the parish rolls of a state church are a legal fiction. Voluntary faith is honest faith. That conviction is the glory of my tradition, and I hold it still.

And now say the other thing, because this is where the era's whole story gathers. A church that cannot compel must persuade. A church that must persuade must gather a crowd, hold its attention, and win its allegiance against every rival, including all the other churches. Disestablishment created, for the first time anywhere, a religious free market, and into that market walked the heirs of Whitefield carrying the toolkit this half-century had assembled: the event, the crowd, the publicity, the celebrity itinerant, the serial story, the technique that gathers thousands. None of those tools was wicked. Every one of them was useful. That is precisely what makes a toolkit dangerous to a church, because tools that work do not wait to be needed. They ask to be used, and then they ask to be trusted, and a church under market pressure will find it steadily harder to tell the difference between what draws a crowd and what saves a soul.

The awakenings were real. Let the record show that this essay believes it: God moved in Northampton and Kingswood and Aldersgate Street, and tens of thousands of lives turned and stayed turned, and the Christianity that carried the next two centuries of English-speaking mission and mercy was born in that fire. Jesus himself refused every attempt to reduce the Spirit's work to a mechanism: "The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit" (John 3:8). The wind was real. And this era, which knew the wind was real, spent fifty years perfecting windmills, and then handed them to a new nation with no established referee except results.

There was another road, and it was open the whole time. Wesley took it: the same fields, the same crowds, and then every awakened soul folded into a small room with a dozen names and a weekly question, the event bound to formation, the fire set in a hearth. It required patience, discipline, and a willingness to count something other than the crowd. It was, and it remains, the harder road, which is why the story this platform has to tell is mostly the story of the other one. The next essay begins at Cane Ridge, where the American experiment picks the tools up and runs. Before you turn to it, sit for a moment with the question the eighteenth century left on the table, because every generation since, including mine, including yours, has had to answer it with less honesty than it deserved. When the wind stops, and the machinery keeps turning, who in the building can tell?

keyFigures.note: Frankfurt pastor whose Pia Desideria (1675) called for small circles, lay Bible reading, and a converted heart inside a cold orthodoxy.

keyFigures.name: Nikolaus von Zinzendorf
keyFigures.note: Count who sheltered Moravian refugees at Herrnhut; their renewal in 1727 sent missionaries across the world and touched Wesley.

keyFigures.name: Jonathan Edwards
keyFigures.note: Northampton pastor who both defended the awakening and disciplined it, testing true affections against mere heat in Religious Affections (1746).

keyFigures.name: George Whitefield
keyFigures.note: Open-air preacher from 1739 and the first transatlantic celebrity, whose publicity methods assembled the modern revival toolkit.

keyFigures.name: John Wesley
keyFigures.note: His heart strangely warmed at Aldersgate in 1738; he bound awakening to formation through class meetings, bands, and discipline.

keyFigures.name: Charles Chauncy
keyFigures.note: Boston minister whose Seasonable Thoughts (1743) made the strongest case against the revival's disorders.

keyFigures.name: Isaac Backus
keyFigures.note: New England Baptist who argued that establishment corrupts the church and helped press America toward full religious liberty.
